**1\. Registration and Login**

This diagram follows the registration and login workflow in Figure 1\. The client checks Local Only mode before any request, and the project server validates the input, stores a salted password hash, verifies credentials, and locks the username after five failed attempts within 15 minutes.

**2\. Local Only Mode**

This diagram follows Figure 2\. Enabling Local Only makes the network gateway refuse new connections and abort in-flight requests within one second, while disabling it re-enables the blocked functions without replaying old requests. In both cases the setting is saved across restarts.

This diagram follows Figure 3\. After confirming the session, the client lists the user's projects, then creates a new project, opens an existing one, or hands over to the join and download workflows. When the previous session ended abnormally, the user can restore the autosaved working copy.

This diagram shows the data the system stores and the rules on it. The role belongs to ProjectMembership, the link between User and Project, because one user can be the Owner of one project and a Viewer of another. 2\. Architecture

The system combines the Model-View-Controller pattern with the Repository pattern to support local desktop work and server-based sharing. The **Presentation layer** contains the source editor, PDF preview, compile log, AI panel with diff view, and the consent, conflict, sharing, and settings dialogs, together with a persistent Local Only indicator. The **Application layer** contains controllers that receive user actions and the services they call: sandboxed compilation, local AI task handling with diff review, cloud PDF summarization with per-request consent, version recording, autosave and recovery, and synchronization. A **Local-Only Guard** sits in front of every outbound connection and blocks login, sharing, synchronization, and cloud summarization while Local Only mode is on; editing, compilation, local AI, and version history keep working. The **Data layer** applies the Repository pattern: each user keeps a complete local copy of the project, and the project server holds the shared copy together with accounts, roles, and sharing links. Collaboration happens through synchronization rather than real-time co-editing. Users pull remote changes, resolve any conflicts in a side-by-side dialog, and push only when their copy is up to date. The server enforces roles independently of the client, so Viewers can never change content. Implementation technologies such as CodeMirror, PDF.js, Electron or Tauri, and Git are candidate choices, not requirements.

**3\. Implemented Features:**

**3.1 Purpose, scope and conventions**

1\. **Purpose.** This part names the features of the Requirements Specification that the team will build and verify before the course ends. It follows IEEE Std 830: each requirement has a unique identifier, is worded with "shall", carries a priority and a verification method, and traces back to the specification.

2\. **Scope.** The delivered product is a desktop LaTeX editor with accounts. It offers editing, sandboxed compilation with a PDF preview, eight local AI tasks with mandatory diff review, cloud PDF summarization with per-request consent, a global Local Only mode, and crash recovery. A small project server provides login and relays summarization requests.

3\. **Selection rule.** A feature is committed when it is a "Must" in the specification (FR-01 to FR-07 and NFR-01 to NFR-08), serves the core needs of the researcher (Dr. Laila) and the student (Omar), and can be verified on the reference machine. This matches risk PR-03.1, which already treats version history, sharing and synchronization as stretch goals.

4\. **Conventions.** "Shall" marks a mandatory statement. Verification codes are those of the specification: T test, D demonstration, I inspection, A analysis. Feature identifiers IF-nn are new labels only; each one cites the FR, NFR and UC identifiers it implements, so this part adds no new requirement.

5\. **Priority classes.** C is committed: complete and verified. S1 and S2 are stretch blocks, started in that order and only after the scope gate in 4.4 is passed.

**3.2 Committed feature requirements**

Eight features are committed. Each statement restates the behaviour of one feature; the cited specification statements stay authoritative for thresholds and error cases.

| ID and feature | The system shall | Implements | Verif. |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| IF-01 Accounts and sessions | let a visitor register a unique username with a policy-compliant password, log in and log out; lock a username for 15 minutes after five failed logins; and end a session after 8 hours of inactivity. | FR-07.1 to 07.5; UC-01 to 03 | T, I |
| IF-02 Project and file management | let an authenticated user create, open, save and delete projects and manage .tex, .bib, .sty, .png, .jpg and .pdf files (up to 500 files and 100 MB), with LaTeX syntax highlighting and role checks enforced by the server. | FR-01.1 to 01.7; UC-05 to 09 | T, D |
| IF-03 Compilation and preview | compile the main file in a sandbox with no network, shell-escape disabled and fixed CPU, memory, disk and time limits; show the PDF and a clickable compile log; keep the last good PDF marked outdated on failure; and cancel a running build when a new one starts. | FR-02.1 to 02.6; UC-10, 11 | T, I |
| IF-04 Local AI tasks | run the eight local AI tasks on the user's device only, on selections of up to 1,000 words (task 8 from the latest compile log), stream the output, allow cancellation, and fail without changing the document. | FR-03.1 to 03.7; UC-12, 13 | T, D, I |
| IF-05 AI output review | present every AI result as a diff that leaves the document unchanged until the user accepts hunks, apply accepted hunks as one undoable edit, and disable acceptance when the source text has changed. | FR-04.1 to 04.4; UC-14 | T, I |
| IF-06 Local Only mode | provide one persistent global setting that makes zero external connections, aborts in-flight requests within 1 second, blocks online functions with an explanatory message, and keeps editing, compilation and local AI working. | FR-06.1 to 06.7; UC-04 | T, D |
| IF-07 Cloud PDF summarization | validate a PDF (at most 20 MB and 100 pages), obtain consent for each request naming the file and the provider, send content to the cloud only for summarization, show the summary read-only, and refuse when Local Only is on. | FR-05.1 to 05.8; UC-15, 16 | T, I |

Three notes apply to the tables above:

1\. **Reduced form until S2.** FR-01.5 lists only the user's own projects, and FR-01.6 is exercised through policy tests with Editor and Viewer fixtures, because shared projects arrive with S2. The role model and the server-side check are built now so S2 only adds invitations.

2\. **Ranking inside committed work.** Three statements are marked Should in the specification: FR-01.7 (syntax highlighting), FR-03.6 (cancel control) and FR-05.8 (no server copy of the PDF). All other committed statements are Must.

3\. **Version recording.** UC-08 step 4 (record a version on save) is delivered with S1, not with IF-02.

**4\. Feasibility:**

**4.1 Technical approach per feature**

1\. **Stack.** The plan uses Electron with TypeScript for the desktop client, CodeMirror 6 for editing, PDF.js for preview and page counts, Docker with a TeX Live image for the sandbox, a llama.cpp server for the local model, and Node.js with a relational database for the project server. The proposal lists the shell and editor as candidates; fixing them now lets six people start without waiting on tool choices.

2\. **One language.** TypeScript on client and server lets any member move between tracks and lets the permission policy and the interface contracts be shared code.

| Feature | Planned approach | Why it is achievable | Risk |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| IF-01 Accounts and sessions | REST API on the project server; Argon2id hashing with a per-user salt; the 10,000-entry common-password list loaded at start; a failed-login counter per username over a 15-minute window; a sliding 8-hour session token; TLS 1.2 or higher at a reverse proxy. | A standard, well-documented pattern with no novel design. | SR-02. 2 |
| IF-02 Project and file management | One local directory per project plus a small local database for metadata; CodeMirror with a LaTeX mode; one validation module for file types and the 500-file and 100 MB limits; a policy module mapping Owner, Editor and Viewer to allowed actions, used by the server API and the client UI. | CodeMirror supplies highlighting, selection and undo; the rest is file handling. | TR-01. 6 |
| IF-03 Compilation and preview | A long-running container started with no network, CPU, memory and disk limits and shell-escape off; latexmk run through docker exec so the sandbox is already warm; the exec is killed on cancel or after 60 s; file-line-error output parsed into clickable log entries; the last good PDF kept in a separate file. | The container flags map one to one onto FR-02.4, and a warm container is how the 10-second build target is reached. | TR-01. 4 |
| IF-04 Local AI tasks | A ModelAdapter interface with one llama.cpp implementation that talks only to 127.0.0.1; the model runs as a separate process; eight task definitions (prompt, input rule, output rule) share one pipeline for validation, streaming and cancellation; Fix LaTeX takes the first error from the parsed log. | Eight tasks are eight prompts over one pipeline, not eight systems. A model of 3 to 4 billion parameters at 4-bit quantization is expected to fit in 3.0 GB; an early benchmark confirms or replaces the choice recorded in A-6. | TR-01. 2, TR-01. 3 |
| IF-05 AI output review | A word-level diff library builds the hunks; a review panel shows them; accepted hunks are applied as one editor transaction so a single undo reverts them; a revision counter detects a stale diff; a test asserts that no path edits text except the accept handler; for tasks 6 to 8 the proposed source is test-compiled before Accept is enabled. | Transactions and undo come with the editor, and the test-compile reuses the IF-03 service. | TR-01. 1 |
| IF-06 Local Only mode | One NetworkGateway in the main process through which every outbound request passes; a lint rule and a CI check forbid network calls anywhere else; an abort registry cancels in-flight requests within 1 s; no telemetry or update check is built in; the setting is stored in a local file and read before the login screen appears. | One choke point is easier to prove than many scattered checks, and a packet capture verifies it. | SR-02. 1 |
| IF-07 Cloud PDF summarization | The client checks type, size and page count and shows the consent dialog; the file goes to the project server, which streams it to the provider and stores nothing; the provider key stays on the server, encrypted at rest and redacted from logs; a 60-second timeout offers Retry. | One relayed HTTP call plus a dialog; page counts come from PDF.js. | SR-02. 3 |
| IF-08 Autosave and recovery | A 60-second timer writes working copies to a recovery folder kept apart from saved files and creates no version; on project open, a newer copy is offered for restoration. | Small and self-contained; verified by killing the process. | None |

**4.2 Work plan and dependencies**

Work follows dependency order, not the calendar: each step starts when the exit condition of the step before it holds.

![][image79]

The foundation fixes three interface contracts and two spikes; six tracks then run in parallel; integration and measurement follow; stretch work waits for the gate.

1\. **Foundation first.** The team agrees the repository layout, continuous integration with automated tests, and three interface contracts: ModelAdapter, NetworkGateway and the compile service. Two spikes run at once: the model against NFR-04 and NFR-06, and the sandbox against NFR-03. A failed spike changes the plan immediately instead of at integration.

2\. **Six tracks, one owner each.** Every track delivers a vertical slice that runs alone against stubs of the other contracts. WS-4 and WS-5 pair up on the AI-to-diff handover, WS-3 and WS-2 on compile-to-editor, and WS-1 and WS-6 on the summarization path.

3\. **Integration in a fixed order.** The editor with the compiler comes first. Then model, diff review and compiler come together, where tasks 6 to 8 test-compile their result before Accept is enabled. The gateway, server relay and summarization come last.

4\. **Early finishers absorb shared work.** WS-1 and WS-2 hold the best-understood slices, so they take on deployment with TLS, log redaction, the test harness and reference-machine runs first.

5\. **Measure while building.** Each statement with verification code T gets its automated test in the same change that implements it. Reference-machine runs start at the first integration instead of at the end.

6\. **Documents move with the code.** The requirements and design documents are updated at the end of every sprint with a change log (PR-03.3).

7\. **Gate, then stretch.** When the scope gate in 4.4 is met, S1 starts with the capacity left, then S2 as one block.

**4.3 Resources and environment**

The plan needs no purchase beyond one summarization API key and one small server; what it does need is access to a 4 GB GPU and time to measure on it.

1\. **Reference machines.** One or two machines matching the reference configuration (4-core CPU at 3 GHz or faster, 16 GB RAM, SSD, NVIDIA GPU with 4 GB VRAM) are designated (PR-03.2). All NFR-03, NFR-04 and NFR-06 runs happen there, at least 20 runs per measurement, shared across members.

2\. **Developer machines.** Every member needs Docker and the TeX Live image to work on compilation. Members without a suitable GPU build the AI tracks against a recorded-response stub of ModelAdapter and run the real model only on a reference machine.

3\. **Server.** One small host with a TLS certificate, deployable with a single command, runs the project server and its database. Automated tests run on every push, as Scenario E describes.

4\. **External service.** One cloud summarization account with a spending cap and a per-user quota (SR-02.3). The key stays on the server and out of the logs.

5\. **Test data.** A fixed compile fixture (5,000 words, 10 figures of at most 1 MB), 30 prompts for each of the 8 task types and 20 papers make 260 inputs. With two reviewers each, NFR-07 needs at most 520 ratings, about 87 per member. The prompts are written during the foundation step so rating starts as soon as outputs exist.

6\. **Licences.** Library and model licences are checked and versions are pinned before first use (TR-01.6).

**4.4 Verification and scope control**

Feasibility is judged against one fixed gate, and scope is reduced in a fixed order so that the gate stays reachable.

**Scope gate for the committed features.** The gate is met when all five conditions hold:

1\. Every statement of IF-01 to IF-08 with verification code T has a passing automated test, and every D and I statement has a recorded demonstration or checklist.

2\. NFR-03, NFR-04 and NFR-06 meet their thresholds on the reference machine over at least 20 runs.

3\. A 30-minute packet capture in Local Only mode shows no non-loopback traffic (NFR-05).

4\. At least 80% of outputs are rated usable by both reviewers for each task type and for cloud summarization (NFR-07).

5\. No document text or credential appears in the server logs (NFR-08, Scenario E).

**Responses to triggers.** When a trigger occurs, the team responds as follows, so that the gate stays reachable.

| If | Then |
| :---- | :---- |
| A spike shows that the model misses NFR-04 or NFR-06 | Switch to a lower quantization, a smaller model or CPU offload behind ModelAdapter. The thresholds stay unchanged (TR-01.2, TR-01.3). |
| Integration of compile, AI and diff runs late | Drop the test-compile check before Accept on tasks 6 to 8\. It is a risk mitigation (TR-01.1), not a requirement; the diff review stays. |
| A committed track falls behind | Reduce the Should statements first: FR-01.7 syntax highlighting, then FR-03.6 cancel control. FR-05.8 stays, because the relay design satisfies it at no extra cost. |
| The gate is still at risk after the tracks finish | Do not start S1. Spend the capacity on defects and measurement evidence. |
| The gate is met with capacity left | Start S1. Start S2 only if the capacity left covers the whole block, since sharing links give nothing to edit without synchronization (TR-01.5). |

**4.5 Feasibility conclusion**

The committed scope of 52 requirements (73.2% of the backlog) is feasible in the time available, and the stretch scope (a further 25.4%) is optional by design.

1\. **Known parts.** Each of the eight features maps to an existing component and a stated verification method (4.1).

2\. **Two real uncertainties.** Speed and memory of a small model on a 4 GB GPU (NFR-04, NFR-06) and output quality (NFR-07) are the least certain results. Both are measured from the first integration on, and the fallback is a smaller or differently quantized model behind ModelAdapter.

3\. **Parallel by design.** Six tracks have one owner each and meet only at three interface contracts, so no track waits for another's finished code.

4\. **Bounded failure.** If no stretch work finishes, the product is still a complete single-user editor with every privacy guarantee of IF-06 and IF-07.

5\. **Largest residual risk.** Late integration of compile, AI and diff review. It is integrated early and in a fixed order (4.2), with the test-compile check as the first thing to drop.

**5\. Risks**

**5.1 Technical risks (TR-01)**

**TR-01.1 Structural corruption of LaTeX syntax**

● **Description:** The local AI service can generate LaTeX that drops a closing brace or alters a command, especially for the insert table, figure caption and fix syntax tasks. If the user accepts such a result, the document stops compiling and trust in the tool drops.

● **Mitigation:** No AI output enters the document without review, and acceptance is applied as one undoable edit (FR-04.2). The fix task must produce source that compiles (NFR-07). The proposed result is test-compiled in the sandbox before the Accept option is enabled.

**TR-01.2 Hallucinations and weaker output from small quantized models**

● **Description:** A small local model has limited reasoning ability. On long or complex input such as outlines or notes, it may change scientific facts or lose the meaning of the text, which is an academic integrity risk.

● **Mitigation:** Every result is shown as a diff and the system makes no silent edits (FR-04). Input is capped at 1,000 words (FR-03.5), and longer text is split into chunks. Output quality is measured on a test set (NFR-07). A larger model can be plugged in through the ModelAdapter on GPUs with more memory.

**TR-01.3 Out-of-memory crashes on the 4 GB GPU**

● **Description:** Model memory use grows with context length, and a real user’s GPU also serves the display and other applications. Exceeding the 4 GB limit mid-session can crash the model runtime or freeze the interface.

● **Mitigation:** The model is capped at 3.0 GB with a 4,096-token context (NFR-06). If the model fails, the system shows an error and leaves the document unchanged (FR-03.7). The model runs as a separate process, so the editor keeps working and can restart it. A lower quantization or CPU offload is the fallback, at the cost of speed.

**TR-01.4 Untrusted LaTeX compiled on the user’s device**

● **Description:** In a shared project, a collaborator’s .tex or uploaded file is compiled on another member’s machine. A malicious file could try to escape the compiler and reach the host system.

● **Mitigation:** Compilation runs in a sandbox container with shell-escape disabled, no network, access to the project directory only, and CPU, memory, disk and time limits (FR-02.4). The container configuration is inspected as part of verification.

**TR-01.5 Merge conflicts and inconsistent state during synchronization**

● **Description:** Two collaborators may change the same file, or the connection may drop in the middle of a push. Either case can lose or duplicate text.

● **Mitigation:** A push is accepted only when the local copy is up to date, and each push is applied in one transaction (FR-10.3, FR-10.6). Conflicts are shown side by side for the user to resolve (FR-10.4). The local copy is committed automatically before each push and merges are three-way. Synchronization is a “Should” feature, so it is the first to be reduced if time runs short.

**TR-01.6 Dependence on third-party components**

● **Description:** The system relies on a local model runtime, a desktop shell, an editor component and a PDF viewer. A license problem, a breaking update or an abandoned library could force rework.

● **Mitigation:** Models stay behind the common ModelAdapter interface, so a model can be replaced without changing the editor. Licenses are checked and library versions are pinned before use.

**TR-01.7 Server as a single point of failure**

● **Description:** Login, sharing and synchronization depend on one project server. Downtime blocks collaboration, and a server failure could lose shared data.

● **Mitigation:** Editing, compilation, local AI and version history work without the server (NFR-09, FR-06.4). Pushes are atomic (FR-10.6), and the server is backed up regularly.

**5.2 Security, privacy and legal risks (SR-02)**

**SR-02.1 Data egress in hybrid pipelines**

● **Description:** The system has two kinds of AI processing: local tasks, which never leave the device, and cloud PDF summarization, which sends a whole file to a third party. A user may confuse the two, or a code path may bypass the controls, and unpublished or copyrighted material could reach a third party.

● **Mitigation:** A single network gateway sits in front of every outbound connection. Cloud use is limited to summarization (FR-05.4), each request needs consent in a dialog naming the provider and the file (FR-05.2), and a persistent indicator shows the Local Only state (FR-06.5). A packet-capture test verifies that Local Only mode makes no external connection (NFR-05).

**SR-02.2 Role enforcement bypassed**

● **Description:** If any request path (editing, push, synchronization or joining through a link) skips the server-side permission check, a Viewer could change content, or a guessed link could grant access.

● **Mitigation:** The server checks the role on every request, independently of the client (FR-01.6, FR-09.6, FR-10.3). Sharing links use tokens of at least 128 bits with expiry and revocation (FR-09.1, FR-09.3). Each role is tested against each server endpoint.

**SR-02.3 API cost and key handling**

● **Description:** The credentials for the cloud summarization service could leak through logs or the interface, and heavy use could run up unexpected costs.

● **Mitigation:** Credentials are stored encrypted and never appear in logs or the interface (NFR-08). Uploads are limited to 20 MB and 100 pages (FR-05.1). Usage is controlled with per-user quotas or by letting users supply their own key.

**5.3 Project risks (PR-03)**

**PR-03.1 Scope too large for the time available**

● **Description:** The product backlog contains 10 functional requirement groups, 9 non-functional requirements and 28 use cases for a team of six, and the project must be delivered by December 1\.

● **Mitigation:** The “Must” requirements (FR-01 to FR-07) are built first, and version history, sharing and synchronization are treated as stretch goals.

**PR-03.2 Test environment**

● **Description:** The performance tests must run on the reference configuration, which includes a 4 GB NVIDIA GPU and 20 runs per measurement. Not every team member may have such a machine.

● **Mitigation:** One or two reference machines are designated, and test runs are shared among the team.

**PR-03.3 Documentation drifting from the implementation**

● **Description:** The requirements and design specifications must be updated every sprint. If they are not, they will no longer match the system.

● **Mitigation:** Both documents are updated at the end of each sprint, with a change log recording what changed.

**6\. Conclusion:**

This proposal describes a LaTeX editor for academic and long-form writing that combines fast editing and compilation, AI writing tools, and role-based sharing. It is designed around the needs of researchers, students, writers, supervisors and developers. Eight AI tasks run entirely on the user’s device, and a global Local Only mode keeps unpublished work from leaving it. Cloud use is limited to summarizing uploaded PDFs, with consent required for every request. A “zero silent edits” rule means AI output reaches a document only after the user accepts it in a diff view. Compilation runs in a sandbox, and the server enforces roles independently of the client. Collaboration works through synchronization rather than real-time co-editing. The main technical, security and project risks are documented with mitigations, and the “Must” requirements are scheduled first to meet the December 1 deadline.
